DDPAI Drops Their Latest Z100 Flagship Dash Cam and They've Outdone Themselves – Starts at $169
13 photos
Photo: DDPAI
With SEMA underway as we speak, countless automotive OEM manufacturers are unveiling the peak of their lineups. One of those teams is DDPAI, a manufacturer of dashcams hitting the market with all they’ve got, and then some.
Earlier this year, we tested a dashcam system from DDPAI. The Z90 Master was that unit, and after we put it to the test, we quickly realized that this brand means business. We even dropped it into a rally car to see if it can take the abuse, and it can.
Well, building upon the success of their Z90 Master , DDPAI has unveiled the Z100 and its Pro and Master variations, which does all the Z90 brought to the table and then some, taking the brand further than ever before.
{fullimg
Already, DDPAI mentions that ever since they hit the scene, they’ve served over 9 million users worldwide, so clearly, they’re doing something right. They have been around since 2013 and showing no signs of slowing down.
DDPAI considers their latest Z100 as their new flagship model, meaning that it showcases the very best this brand has to offer, and we begin our exploration of the dashboard-mounted machine by taking a closer look at its design.
First and foremost, the Z90 was a system that could be set up to operate on a 24/7 basis by drawing power from your vehicle’s battery in order to offer protection around the clock. However, this ability was only unlocked when using the 4G module that the Z90 included, a separate piece of hardware that you had to mount and wire.
{fullimg
Well, for the Z100, DDPAI has taken that module and incorporated it, among others, into the mounting bracket that you stick to your windshield in order to secure the Z100 in place. They did this to take some hassle out of the setup, which, from my own experience, I appreciate heavily; I had a difficult time mounting the module for the Z90.
That mounting bracket is what you see with a bit of a red strip lining the upper edge, which also incorporates the GPS module and wires for powering the Z100.
Another major difference we can see is that the Z100 also includes multiple lenses, toward the front, not just one, and it’s this feature that takes the Z100 to the next level. The benefits here are an ultra-wide angle of capture, and “telephoto views” of whatever the road ahead has to offer.
The wide-angle lens operates with a 4K resolution and is able to capture up to four lanes of traffic, and the telephoto lens runs at 2K. These specs are then coupled with a 4X+ optical zoon and 86 mm (equivalent) focal length. This allows the Z100 to also capture crystal-clear images of license plates from as far as 60 m (197 ft) away and an effective visibility of 100 m (328 ft).
{fullimg
According to a press release from DDPAI, the Z100 also has a few other tricks up its sleeve, one of which is an auto-adapting “dark to bright” aperture. At the front, the system switches between F1.0 and F2.0 without any manual adjusting required, ensuring that glare is limited during the day and at night, capturing as much light as possible, all in the name of ensuring that you and parties involved in an accident, know precisely what happened.
Keep in mind, however, that there are rear cameras that are to be coupled with the Z100 too, one that checks out what’s happening behind your vehicle, and another in the cabin.
Keep in mind that all of the cameras , including the master unit, include Sony’s Starvis 2 IMX678, 1/1.8-inch sensor with 8 MP, and just like the master, they’ll record at 4K. All three channels support HDR footage too, so exposure is balanced constantly, including glare and headlight reflections.
{fullimg
Furthermore, the ecosystem is completed with features like voice activation and control, along with 5G video transfers of footage to other devices, overheating protection, an integrated display on the backside of the Z100 Master, and if I’m not mistaken, infrared imaging inside the cabin at night.
If that last one is anything like the Z90, I can say that you’ll be surprised by how powerful the infrared is. When we tested the Z90, we could literally see our veins in the footage, which, if you ask me, is pretty mind-blowing. Let’s not forget about app controls.
The question is: How much cash will we need to get our hands on this piece of gear? According to our correspondence at DDPAI, in its least expensive variation, the Z100 rolls in with a price of $169 (€150). This is for the standard Z100 with a complete Z100 Master setup with three cameras and hardwire kit, rolling in at $539 (€480).
If you’re at SEMA during this period, DDPAI’s stall is located in the North Hall and sitting at #10861. They’re also carrying out reviews and tests on site too, so you can mess with the gear before you actually purchase it. Keep in mind that events such as these also entice clients to purchase products with an array of price cuts and deals to hook us, and that’s a win for anyone looking for a new dash cam; DDPAI confirms better offers at SEMA.

Sales of assets from Seagen and Biohaven grew in the third quarter, but it wasn’t enough for Pfizer to overcome declines across the Prevnar and COVID franchises.
While Pfizer’s revenue did not rise in the third quarter, the New York pharma pointed to rising sales of launched and acquired products as evidence of a sustained effort to drive longer-term growth.
The company reported revenue of $16.6 billion, compared to $16.7 billion for the same period a year ago, according to a Tuesday release . Without including its COVID products, which have been on the decline post-pandemic, Pfizer’s revenue grew 7% operationally, the company reported.
“This quarter, our non-COVID products delivered strong 7% operational revenue growth, and I’m particularly pleased with the 32% year-over-year operational revenue growth from our launched and acquired products,” said Cecile Guegan, who was introduced as Pfizer’s new CFO on Tuesday morning.
Analysts were similarly optimistic, with Guggenheim calling the third quarter performance solid since revenue beat expectations of $16.15 billion.
“Beyond the quarterly results, the main focus for investors on the Pfizer story is the evolution of the company’s pipeline, which we believe remains underappreciated,” Guggenheim wrote on Tuesday morning.
Vaccines

The acquired products that contributed heavily to the quarter include those from Seagen, Metsera and Biohaven. Products from antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) specialist Seagen, acquired in a 2023 deal valued at $43 billion , grew 39% year over year, Pfizer reported. Key product Padcev brought in $255 million globally, a 55% increase. Pfizer attributed this to increased market share in first-line locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer and a launch in muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
Metsera, on the other hand, has yet to contribute to earnings with no approved products, but Pfizer noted that 10 pivotal studies have been advanced so far this year for lead asset berobenatide.
Migraine drug Nurtec, from the 2022 Biohaven acquisition , achieved 33% revenue growth year over year for $135 million in the quarter.
Pfizer’s own Eliquis, a key product nearing its patent cliff, grew 25% for $513 million.
But the COVID portfolio dragged on earnings, as expected. For COVID, Paxlovid declined by $771 million, or 63%, as infections slowed in the U.S. and globally. BioNTech-partnered vaccine Comirnaty fell $339 million, or 29%.
Despite the drops, both products were “modest contributors” to Pfizer’s overall 5% topline beat, BMO Capital Markets said in a Tuesday morning note, outperforming consensus estimates by 1% and 22%, respectively.
Pneumococcal vaccine family Prevnar also saw steep declines of $180 million, or 10%, as vaccination rates in the U.S. dropped and competitors loomed.
CEO Albert Bourla, who will speak to investors on a 10 a.m. ET earnings call, promised in the release that Pfizer has growth ahead, particularly in obesity, oncology, immunology and vaccines.
Further underscoring Bourla’s confidence, Pfizer has raised its full year revenue by $1.5 billion, with the revenue range now $62–64 billion. This is up from $60.5–$62.5 billion previously, per BMO.

source_document.body:
Some of the most valuable real estate in the U.S. energy system is hidden in plain sight: the utility corridor. These narrow strips of land carry high-voltage alternating current (HVAC) transmission lines across farmland, suburbs, and industrial parks. They have become increasingly important as it becomes harder to add lines to new land.
Building transmission lines in new corridors can take 10 to 15 years, largely because of permitting tied to land acquisition and environmental review. To increase capacity within existing right-of-way (ROW), utilities are replacing legacy conductors in HVAC systems with advanced ones that can carry far more power on the same towers. This reconductoring and energizing process typically raises a line’s capacity by 50% to 110% in 18 to 36 months. A 2024 GridLab analysis found that, when construction of new energy transmission corridors is constrained, adding reconductoring could deliver nearly four times as much new grid transmission capacity by 2035 as building new lines alone.
COMMENTARY
The approach is already proving itself. In 2024, Salt River Project reconductored an 8.5-mile, 230-kV line near Phoenix, Arizona, raising its continuous rating by roughly 80% in about 18 months while reusing the line’s 1970s-era towers.
Federal policy is set to accelerate the shift to reconductoring. In September 2026, the U.S. Dept. of Energy announced $1.9 billion for 31 projects under its SPARK program. Combined with about $3.4 billion in project sponsor contributions, the planned investment totals approximately $5.3 billion to reconductor or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of HVAC transmission lines and deploy grid-enhancing technologies across nearly 21,000 additional miles. Together, they are expected to add 23 GW of additional transmission capacity on existing right-of-way.
The Corridor Has Multiple Tenants
This is a promising solution, but one potential challenge is that those corridors are often shared. Power lines run overhead, and oil and gas (O&G) pipelines frequently run beneath or alongside them. Co-location makes sense because it limits land disturbance, but it also means different owners may be responsible for what happens above and below ground.
HVAC transmission lines and O&G pipelines may fall under different regulatory requirements and be managed by separate integrity and corrosion engineering teams, whether they belong to different companies or divisions within the same company. Coordinating across those teams is essential when an upgrade changes conditions in a shared corridor. The challenge is adding capacity overhead while addressing the impact it may have on everything else (assets and facilities) in the right-of-way.
HVAC transmission line upgrades call for planning across the entire utility corridor. Source: AMPP (used with permission)
How Higher Operating Currents Can Affect Nearby Pipelines
A buried steel pipeline running near an HVAC transmission line can experience alternating current (AC)-induced voltage and current. As reconductoring increases the line’s current-carrying and operating capacity, AC interference on a nearby pipeline will also increase, depending on the configuration of the power line and pipeline and the mitigation already in place.
AC interference presents two concerns: personnel safety and pipeline corrosion. The first is safety. Induced voltage can create shock hazards for crews working on or near the pipeline. Industry practice under the NACE SP0177 standard uses 15 V AC as the steady-state touch-voltage threshold, and IEEE Standard 80 sets criteria for assessing touch and step voltages during fault conditions. The second is corrosion. Pipelines rely on protective coatings and cathodic protection (CP) to keep buried steel from corroding. Where induced AC finds a small coating defect, it can discharge into the soil and accelerate corrosion at that spot. Voltage, in this case, is not the best indicator of corrosion. A 2015 DNV GL report for the INGAA Foundation notes that when the 15 V AC threshold is used, it “considers personnel safety and does not necessarily address corrosion issues.”
Corrosion risk depends more directly on AC current density at coating defects “holidays” than on voltage alone. ISO 18086 provides criteria for evaluating AC corrosion risk on cathodically protected pipelines. An HVAC power load increase can create a corrosion concern even while voltage readings remain within personnel-safety limits.
A Neighbor’s Upgrade Affects Everyone
A pipeline operator may need to respond to changes made by neighboring utilities. Federal regulation anticipates this scenario under 49 CFR 192.473(c), which requires onshore gas transmission operators to conduct interference surveys when new stray-current sources appear. This includes HVAC power lines with “a voltage up-rating, added lines” or additional generation. Operators must develop a remedial action plan when AC interference current density reaches or exceeds 100 A/m², or when interference impedes safe pipeline operation or could adversely affect the environment or the public.
That trigger assumes the pipeline operator knows something has changed. A same-voltage reconductoring isn’t named explicitly in the regulation, but monitoring indicates a significant increase in stray current triggers a requirement for an interference survey. Because reconductoring stays within existing right-of-way, it can often proceed with limited siting review. In this scenario, handoff communication between electric utilities companies and pipeline operators becomes vital to risk mitigation.
Technical guidance exists on both sides, from IEEE 2746 for electric transmission owners to NACE SP0177 and SP21424 for pipeline operators. Early coordination between electric transmission owners and pipeline operators should be part of reconductoring planning.
A related California HVAC power transmission upgrade illustrates how operators can account for a neighboring pipeline. In 2025, Southern California Edison reported that it did not intend to operate the Lugo-Mohave transmission line at the full compensation provided by its Eldorado-Lugo-Mohave upgrade until AC mitigation work on SoCalGas pipelines was complete. The two companies were working together on the scope, schedule and cost of that mitigation.
Planning Beyond the Asset Owners
Utility corridors cross communities, and the stakes extend beyond the asset owners. A related shared-corridor example comes from Puget Sound Energy’s Energize Eastside project , which upgraded a 16-mile transmission corridor from 115 kV to 230 kV through four Seattle-area suburbs. Sharing the corridor with two Olympic Pipe Line petroleum pipelines, the project’s 2016 planning study demonstrated how asset owners can assess safety when major infrastructure systems operate side by side.
Pipeline safety was a concern during the permitting process. A 2016 AC interference study commissioned by Puget Sound Energy evaluated how different transmission line configurations and routes could affect the nearby pipelines. The study recommended selecting a configuration that reduced interference and conducting field monitoring after the line was energized. The project also included continued coordination with the pipeline operator and additional safety measures during design and construction.
Mitigation itself can involve landowners. Installing grounding systems or gradient-control wire can require trenching along the pipeline, so an upgrade within an existing right-of-way may still involve ground disturbance.
Planning For the Whole Corridor
None of these challenges are arguments against reconductoring. It is one of the fastest, most land-efficient ways to add capacity. In any reconductoring project, capacity planning should account for the whole corridor. Planning for the whole corridor also means considering how an incident involving one asset could affect neighboring infrastructure and operations. This includes notifying co-located operators early when a line’s loading or rating will change, sharing load data, jointly modeling interference before re-energizing, budgeting mitigation into project costs, and confirming results with surveys before and after.
Transmission owners and pipeline operators should coordinate early so interference assessment, integrity and corrosion management and any necessary mitigation are part of the upgrade plan.
— Tim Gonzalez is vice president of Energy Integrity Solutions for the Association for Materials Protection and Performance .

BYD’s electric supercar delivers an insane nearly 3,000 hp from four electric motors. During a high-speed test, the Yangwang U9 Extreme crashed at about 280 mph, but the driver walked away unharmed.
BYD shares video of EV supercar in high-speed crash
The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is a “dream car,” as BYD calls it, a souped-up, track-focused version of its electric hypercar.
After it became the world’s fastest production car last year, reaching a top speed of 496.22 km/h, or about 308 mph, BYD is attempting to beat it by breaking the 500 km/h (310 mph) mark.
The Yangwang U9 Xtreme features the world’s first mass-produced 1,200V ultra-high-voltage platform and BYD’s e4 platform.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The quad-motor setup is the first in the world rated at 30,000 rpm, BYD said, delivering nearly 3,000 hp (3,000 PS) combined.
While BYD is preparing to attempt a run this month, the company shared a video of the Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing in a violent high-speed test.
During the first run, it clocked over 350 km/h (217 mph), no problem. On the second run, it hit over 420 km/h (261 mph).
However, during the third run, BYD was attempting to reach over 450 km/h (280 mph) when the vehicle violently crashed into the guardrail and continued spinning out of control. You can see some of the footage from inside the vehicle.
BYD said that after a comprehensive medical exam, the hospital found the driver in good health with no serious injuries.
BYD Yangwang U9 Xtreme (Source: Yangwang)
The vehicle’s high-strength carbon-fiber cabin also held up impressively despite the front and rear damage.
It didn’t take long for BYD to try again, reaching a top speed of 457.89 km/h (284.5 mph) on the next run. Jiang Gong, one of Yangwang’s riders, said he sees some leeway and believes it can break 500 km/h (310 mph).
At the end of the video, BYD said (translated into English), “The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached.”

Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.
The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.
The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.
There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Zero Project Ventura: A new electric motorcycle for under $8,000
Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that Zero hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.
With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.
And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.
The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).
That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.
Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.
We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the smallest of electric motorcycles that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.
Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.
The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.
Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as a potential gateway to motorcycle ownership.
“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.
That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.
Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.
But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.
Zero XE electric dirt bike is finally going street-legal
Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.
The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles , offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.
Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.
The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.
Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.
The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.
For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.
That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.
The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.
Zero LS3 electric scooter makes its European debut
Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.
While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.
The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.
Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.
Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.
That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.
The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.
Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.
The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.
Zero is developing a completely new smartphone app
Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.
The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.
One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.
The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.
An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.
Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.
Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.
Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.
The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.
DC fast charging is finally coming to more Zero motorcycles
Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging .
Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.
The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.
That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.
Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.
European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.
The latter is particularly interesting given the growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America , potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.
Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.
The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.
Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.
Electrek’s Take
There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.
For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.
Now we’re seeing a different approach.
The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.
I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.
That’s an audience I’ve been watching grow for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.
For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.
The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.
And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.
Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.
But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.
And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.

If the new ReBake Abler electric motorcycle looks like it might share a bit of DNA with Sweden’s dearly departed CAKE, there’s a good reason for that.
ReBake Motors has officially unveiled its first electric two-wheeler at EICMA 2026 in Milan, introducing the Abler as a highly modular, utility-focused electric moped and light motorcycle.
Behind the new Swedish company is founder and CEO Karl Ytterborn, who spent eight years at CAKE from its founding in 2016 through 2024. CAKE famously built some of the most interesting minimalist electric motorcycles and utility bikes on the market before ultimately collapsing after failing to secure additional funding. Ytterborn says ReBake is intended to apply many of the lessons learned during that experience, while eliminating unnecessary cost and complexity.
And the Abler certainly looks the part.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Its chunky 42mm aluminum tube frame isn’t just a styling exercise. ReBake designed it as a mounting system, allowing cargo accessories to attach directly to the frame at multiple locations. That means riders can configure the bike for everything from carrying groceries and passengers to more serious utility duties.
There are two versions. The Abler45 is an EU L1e-B moped with a 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed, 4 kW nominal motor and 5.12 kW peak output. It starts at €3,990 including VAT.
The €4,990 Abler80 steps up to the A1 light motorcycle category, increasing nominal power to 6.14 kW and peak power to 7.68 kW while pushing the top speed beyond 80 km/h (50 mph). Both versions use a direct-drive rear hub motor.
Energy comes from removable 2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries weighing 17 kg (37.5 lb) apiece. The Abler45 comes standard with one battery but can carry two, while the Abler80 includes two for 4 kWh of total capacity. With both batteries, ReBake claims up to 160 km (99 miles) of low-speed urban range on the Abler45 or 114 km (71 miles) on the Abler80. Each battery can be charged either on or off the bike from a normal 230V outlet, reaching a full charge in four hours.
The rest of the hardware includes 14-inch cast wheels, 140mm of front suspension travel, dual rear shocks, front and rear disc brakes with combined braking, regenerative braking, and full LED lighting.
Perhaps more interesting than any individual specification, though, is simply seeing another Swedish electric motorcycle startup emerge from CAKE’s ashes.
CAKE demonstrated that there was plenty of appetite for unconventional, lightweight electric motorcycles. Unfortunately, it also demonstrated just how difficult it is to turn that enthusiasm into a sustainable business.
ReBake appears to be getting another crack at that equation – this time with eight years’ worth of lessons already baked in.

FedEx Corp.’s recent strategy to focus more on specialized services for companies in industrial sectors with complex logistics requirements, beyond basic parcel delivery, is paying dividends, especially in the aerospace and automotive sectors.
The freight transportation giant last week described how it secured a series of new customer wins after integrating disparate capabilities across global parcel, freight, freight forwarding, and trade compliance services under one umbrella, with dedicated teams able to develop customized solutions.
FedEx ( NYSE: FDX ), for example, created a dedicated logistics process for quickly and reliably moving aircraft engines and oversized aircraft components to help airlines complete maintenance, and minimize time out of service. Since June 2025, FedEx has transported hundreds of aircraft engines, according to a company news release. CEO Raj Subramaniam said during the third-quarter earnings call that engine moves increased 15-fold from prior levels.
Many large freight forwarders have so-called Aircraft on Ground logistics services that support aviation and aerospace companies, including overhaul facilities and suppliers, facing urgent operational disruptions. Speed is critical when an airplane is grounded in need of repair, a manufacturer is missing components to keep the assembly line running or a repair facility discovers unexpected damage during a scheduled maintenance check and doesn’t have the part on hand. Experts also say expediting an urgent shipment requires synchronization between logistics partners, the buyer and quality teams.
Demand for engine transport has increased in recent years as new-generation engines prove less durable and get removed from the wing to be sent to manufacturers for repair. Airlines are also keen to maximize fleet availability because supply chain and regulatory headwinds have slowed airframers ability to deliver new orders on time. That means airlines are holding on longer to aging aircraft, creating a greater need for specialized logistics support during unexpected aircraft downtime, critical parts shortages, unplanned maintenance events and other operational challenges.
Logistics companies with AOG desks offer around-the-clock access to dedicated teams that can quickly arrange transportation, make routing decisions and manage regulatory requirements for shipments under tight time pressure. Other advantages typically include the ability to follow customer-specific operating procedures; provide flexible transportation options, such as next-flight out, dedicated trucking, and charter flights; access to a global network of offices and facilities; and enhanced monitoring and customer communication throughout the shipment lifecycle.
Seattle-based Expeditors International last summer said it expanded its AOG services. Other companies with significant AOG logistics operations include Kuehne+Nagel and Ceva Logistics. In February, K+N acquired Ireland-based Eastway Global Forwarding Ltd., which specializes in AOG services, aircraft engine logistics, aviation logistics & warehousing, and customs brokerage services.
“When an aircraft engine needs to move, every hour matters and every detail counts,” Marcus Balzereit, the new president of FedEx Logistics, said in the news release. “A delayed engine can impact flight schedules, aircraft availability, maintenance schedules, and operational commitments across the aviation industry. With our own airline DNA, we understand firsthand the complexity and urgency behind keeping aircraft flying. Our solution brings together dedicated aerospace experts, digital innovation, and a proven global network to provide customers with the speed, visibility, and reliability they need to keep operations running efficiently.”
Balzereit was promoted Aug. 3 to lead FedEx Logistics, the freight forwarding unit at FedEx that manages shipments for customers using FedEx and third-party carriers. He previously was senior vice president of Asia Pacific sales and solutions.
His mandate is to deepen FedEx’s industry expertise and develop tailored solutions to help key B2B customers optimize supply chain operations, according to the news release announcing his appointment.
The aerospace support center, for example, manages all quotations for booking engines on freighter aircraft and oversees handling and transportation from origin to destination — much like any freight agent. Working closely with colleagues around the world, the experts provide centralized oversight, regulatory compliance, customs coordination and end-to-end accountability throughout a shipment’s journey. Complementing the process is a proprietary digital platform that streamlines quotation generation, automates communication and securely manages shipment documentation, FedEx said in last week’s news release.
Automotive and cloud computing
As part of the focus on high- margin , premium services, FedEx last year began offering more differentiated services for the automotive production market, with a dedicated team, 24/7 support, flexible global pickup capabilities, and enhanced visibility. The effort paid off in the third quarter when it began serving 13 major automotive customers, Chief Commercial Officer Brie Carere said on the earnings call.
The AI and data center industry was the fastest growing vertical at FedEx during the third quarter quarter. A recent Frost & Sullivan report , sponsored by FedEx, discussed how AI is influencing trade patterns in the Asia-Pacific region and trans-Pacific freight movements, which FedEx is capitalizing on.
Healthcare revenue grew by double digits in the quarter. In July, FedEx established a life sciences division to coordinate specialized healthcare logistics operations.
“Our expanding capabilities across key verticals are enabling us to address more of our customers’ logistic needs, unlocking air freight demand from traditionally parcel-centric customers,” Subramaniam said. “Differentiation is increasingly centered on deep customer relationships and tailored service experiences, positioning us to capture more freight volume as we address customers’ needs beyond parcel.”

Aprilia Obscure Spe.Ed. Is an Even Lighter RSV4 with Leg Wings, Just 500 to Be Made
9 photos
Photo: autoevolution/Cristian Curmei
Italian bike maker Aprilia is one of the most unforgiving forces in two-wheeled motorsport. The company has no less than 54 titles to its name in various competitions, so when it announces a new version of a bike that was responsible for seven of those titles in the World Superbike Championship, the world is bound to pay attention.
That bike would be the mighty RSV4 , a platform that has been periodically honored with more and more extreme versions of itself. Taking advantage of the Esposizione Internazionale Ciclo Motociclo e Accessori (EICMA) show in Milan, Italy, which opens its doors this week, a new such version, perhaps the most extreme one yet, comes under the spotlight.
They call it the RSV4 Obscure Spe.Ed., and it is supposed to be a limited-edition version (only 500, each of them numbered, are being planned) designed specifically, but not exclusively, for the racetrack.
The main focus of the Italian engineers fell on making the motorcycle as light as possible. Since there weren't all that many things that could be removed to cut weight, Aprilia went for carbon fiber parts wherever possible, including the mudguards, side panels, footrest guards, and front brake air intakes.
The bike shed the most pounds off its wheels, with the new carbon ones being 4.4 pounds (two kg) lighter than the wheels fitted on the RSV4 Factory. In all, the total weight of the Obscure Spe.Ed. Is 6.6 pounds (three kg) less than the Factory version.
That would be a total of 432 pounds (196 kg) for the newcomer, when the ART (Aprilia Racing Technology) exhaust system is fitted. Without it, the motorcycle tips the scales at 443 pounds (201 kg).
But cutting weight is not the only way one can make a bike faster and more effective on the track. Aerodynamic elements matter, too, and it is here that Aprilia likes to play the toughest game.
For the new version of the RSV4, Aprilia imagined something called leg wings, carbon fiber extra fittings designed to increase downforce by up to 20 percent. Already previewed on the RS-GP prototype, the solution makes its debut on a production limited edition superbike.
The heart of the two-wheeled monster continues to be the same engine that powers the RSV4 and RSV4 Factory, a narrow-V four-cylinder powerplant the bike maker likes to call a world first.
As the company's most powerful engine ever, the 1,099cc piece of tech is rated at 220 hp at 13,000 rpm and 127 Nm of torque at 10,800 rpm. When riders opt for the ART exhaust system, those numbers jump to 223 hp and almost 132 Nm of torque.
The suspension system on the Obscure Spe.Ed. Is new as well, and it consists of an Ohlins NIX fork at the front and an Ohlins TTX shock at the rear. These elements tie into wheels measuring 17 inches on both ends.
Aprilia says it will offer the RSV4 Obscure Spe.Ed. (that funky word is supposed to be a contraction of Special Edition) in a single color, black all over, but makes no mention of how much it will charge for one of these babies. Knowing this company, though, it will probably not be cheap.
Especially if you take into account that this new version has now become the new flagship of the RSV4 range.

Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO November 3, 2026
I-80 Gold (TSX: IAU; NYSE: IAUX) expects annual production in the lower half of its forecast range after worker turnover slowed mining in Nevada, even as the company’s next underground operation approaches a year-end start. The stock dropped.
Toronto-based i-80 maintained its 40,000–50,000 oz. outlook but flagged delayed access to high-grade ore at Granite Creek and a processing change that shifts some gold from the Archimedes mine into early 2027. Production mining at Archimedes and the refurbishment of the Lone Tree processing plant remain on schedule, i-80 said in its quarterly update Monday.
“The contractor workforce has since been restored to previous staffing levels to support planned mining rates following an adjustment to contractor compensation structure,” chief operating officer Paul Chawrun said in the release.
The setbacks highlight the operating demands behind i-80’s plan to lift annual gold output to 150,000–200,000 oz. starting in 2028. Its Lone Tree restart would allow the company to process its own refractory ore, which requires treatment to release gold trapped in sulphide minerals, and retain more of the margin now paid to third parties.
I-80 shares fell 2.9% to $1.88 Tuesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about $1.6 billion (US$1.1 billion). They’ve traded between $1.25 and $3.04 in the past year.
Cash and growth
I-80’s third-quarter net loss widened to US$48.4 million ($67.8 million), or US6¢ a share, from US$41.9 million, or US5¢, as development and exploration expenses increased, according to Monday’s statement.
Quarterly output fell 6% from a year earlier to 11,685 oz., while revenue edged higher to US$32.7 million as stronger gold prices offset fewer ounces sold.
I-80 had cash and cash equivalents of US$411.4 million as of Sept. 30, down from US$464.6 million three months earlier. National Bank Financial calculated potential liquidity of roughly US$620 million including a conditional US$100-million expansion of the gold-prepayment arrangement and about US$109 million from the exercise of warrants whose exercise prices were below the share price.
National Bank Financial mining analyst Don DeMarco maintained his outperform rating and $4 target in a note Monday evening. Despite the near-term production weakness, development remains funded and on schedule, he said.
Lone Tree spending
Lone Tree remains the central investment in i-80’s growth plan. First gold is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2027 following a refurbishment budgeted at about US$430 million.
Labour costs are running 5%–10% above initial estimates, though they remain within the project contingency. About 44% of capital has been committed and 20% of contingency drawn, according to DeMarco. The contingency draw compares with roughly 10% cited in a development update last month, he noted.
Payments on Lone Tree contracts are being made four to five months after commitments, against an originally assumed 30 days, moving expenditure into 2027, DeMarco said.
Mineral Point
Beyond Lone Tree, i-80 has moved Mineral Point ahead of the Granite Creek open pit and Cove underground project in its development sequence. The change concentrates spending on its largest growth project while reserving Cove as a later source of processing-plant feed.
An Archimedes feasibility study and Mineral Point prefeasibility study are now expected in the second half of 2027, a modest shift from the previous mid-year targets, DeMarco noted.
“In our view, continued execution at Granite Creek, Archimedes and Lone Tree can progressively de-risk the development pipeline and narrow the gap between asset value and market valuation,” he said.
Labour and water
Staffing was already a concern last month during an analyst visit. Granite Creek’s mining contractor had about 100 employees against a target of roughly 120 amid strong competition for skilled workers in northern Nevada, SCP Resource Finance said in an Oct. 26 note.
The mine had enough working areas to support higher output, but labour availability and the speed of the mining cycle were the constraints, SCP said. Water management remained another challenge, with deeper pumping wells and expanded treatment capacity expected to help the ramp-up.
While Granite Creek’s September feasibility study established initial gold reserves and a larger resource, it also raised projected life-of-mine all-in sustaining costs 42% from the previous assessment to US$2,273 ($3,177) per ounce.
At Archimedes, placing oxide ore on the existing Ruby Hill leach pad instead of selling it to a third party is expected to defer recognition of some production until the first quarter of 2027. That distinction leaves the year-end mining start intact while delaying some reported gold output.

Hot Honda CBR1000RR-R Fireblade Gets Even Hotter With 2027 Mechanical and Visual Upgrades
56 photos
Photo: Honda
Japanese bike maker Honda has a product so successful and intense that it rarely needs to do anything to it to keep it relevant. Yet, as impressive as it is, the CBR1000RR-R Fireblade does need a refresh from time to time, and that's exactly what its maker announced this week at the EICMA show in Milan, Italy.
The last time Honda made some serious upgrades to the two-wheeler was a couple of years ago, but now, with all the deep changes announced this week, we'll need to reset the clock on that.
Although basically the same 1,000cc sports motorcycle as it's been over the past few years, the 2027 Honda CBR1000RR-R Fireblade throws in many new things, both internally and externally, so it's definitely worth a closer look.
As the base of tried and tested race bikes, the new Fireblade makes use of the same frame as before, but with modified rigidity balance and steering geometry, and accompanied by a lighter swingarm.
The suspension system stays the same Showa setup as before, but the forks and shock now tie into new and lighter 17-inch wheels, which are both equipped with Nissin braking hardware.
It's in the engine department that the most changes have been made. Even if they don't really alter the powerplant's performance levels, they are meant to make the Fireblade an even more unstoppable beast on the track.
The bike's liquid-cooled inline four-cylinder heart is good for 215 hp at 14,000 rpm and 114 Nm of torque at 10,500 rpm, but it now utilizes variable air funnels, throttle-by-wire, and revised cam timing, among other things.
On a hardware level, the 1,000cc engine got fitted with magnesium covers, aluminum bolts, and new crankcases – all of them selected as a means for the motorcycle to drop some weight – more specifically, 2.2 pounds (one kg) compared to the 2024 model year Fireblade.
To go with the few revisions to the bodywork, Honda opted to gift the bike with a brand-new aero package. It looks different from what it used to, but it does the same job as the previous setup – and Honda admitted as much.
Developed with assistance from the HRC WorldSBK team, the package swaps the previous winglet design for the fairing for a mid-section aero device. Apparently, the new solution delivers the same levels of downforce as before.
Honda installed a new LED headlight up front, redrew the front spoiler, remade the 4.4-gallon (16.6 liters) fuel tank in titanium, and raised the seat height a bit. Additionally, it also installed new lower cowl aerodynamic sidepods.
The Japanese do not specifically say when the world will get to meet the new Honda beast, but they did share that the 2027 model year will be offered both as the CBR1000RR-R Fireblade SP and CBR1000RR-R Fireblade HRC Works Edition. We're waiting for pricing to be revealed so that we can tell you that as well.

The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.
First teased last week , the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version that we originally reviewed , opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.
And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.
Eli ZERO MX: Same tiny car, more power
The Eli ZERO MX retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.
The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.
That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.
The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.
Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.
Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.
There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.
The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.
The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.
For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.
A sporty Race Edition with a hidden surprise
Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.
The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.
Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.
Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.
But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.
Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.
Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.
It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.
Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.
Small electric cars finding their place
Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.
The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.
By expanding into the L7e category, Eli is addressing one of the biggest limitations of its original design: speed.
A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.
The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.
Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.
Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.
For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

Two groups behind construction of a proposed $1-billion natural gas-fired power plant in northern Wisconsin told state officials they are pulling the plug on the project. Dairyland Power Cooperative, headquartered in La Crosse, Wisconsin, and South Shore Energy—a subsidiary of Allete—the parent of Minnesota Power—in a letter to Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission told commissioners the groups would not move forward with the Nemadji Trail Energy Center (NTEC).
The power plant was sited in Superior, in Douglas County, near Lake Superior, and also near Duluth, Minnesota. The letter to the PSC was filed Oct. 28 by Daniel McCourtney, manager of strategic environmental initiatives at Allete, which had distanced itself from the project late last year.
“No construction has occurred on NTEC or the [generation tie line],” McCourtney wrote in the letter to the PSC. “Accordingly, the owners respectfully request that the commission acknowledge their relinquishment of all rights associated with the [plant approvals].”
This is a rendering of the proposed Nemadji Trail Energy Center in Wisconsin. Construction of the natural gas-fired power plant, which was approved in 2020, was canceled in October 2026. Courtesy: Dairyland Power Cooperative
The PSC had approved the project in 2020. The commission had granted certificates of public convenience and necessity for construction of a natural gas-fired power plant with generation capacity of between 550 and 625 MW. The utilities had proposed the NTEC as a way to provide baseload electricity to replace retiring coal-fired generation, and support power reliability as they made more investments in renewable energy.
Several Gas-Fired Power Stations Move Forward
Other gas-fired power plant projects are moving forward in Wisconsin. Regulators recently approved Invenergy’s request to build two new gas-fired stations in the southern part of the state, and We Energies—the state’s largest electric utility—has said it would buy the plants. The Red Oak Ridge Energy Center project would be a nearly 1.2-GW facility; the Foundry Ridge Energy Center would have 324 MW of generation capacity.
We Energies also received approval in 2025 for two new gas-fired facilities, in Oak Creek (1,100 MW) and Paris (128 MW). POWER previously reported on the utility’s plan to build a gas-fired plant in Outagamie County; the Fox North Energy Center would have 750 MW of generation capacity.
Invenergy in August filed an engineering plan with the PSC for two gas-fired stations in Calumet County in northeast Wisconsin that would have a combined generation capacity of nearly 2 GW. We Energies has included the power plants in its regulatory filings, and has said the 1,200-MW Forest Junction Energy Center and the 750-MW Union Depot Energy Center could be online by December 2031.
Legal Challenges
Indigenous and environmental groups, including Clean Wisconsin and the Sierra Club, had filed legal challenges against the NTEC facility . The groups also had asked the state’s Supreme Court to hear a lawsuit that challenged the PSC’s approval of the plant, though the court declined to take the case. There also was local opposition, and the NTEC also had permitting delays .
Jennifer Cady, vice president of public policy for Minnesota Power, in a December filing to the PSC said that air, wetland, and construction permits for the project had expired due to delays. Minnesota Power also nixed an agreement with its subsidiary South Shore Energy to buy power from the plant.
City officials in Superior also had denied approval for the plant, amid concerns from local residents about noise and pollution, and the impact on surrounding wetlands. Regional tribes and environmental groups also raised those concerns. The plant’s location would have been near a cemetery in Superior in which some 200 ancestors of the Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa are buried.
Project supporters had said the facility would have benefited the area with about 350 jobs during construction, and another two dozen full-time jobs once in operation. Officials who supported the plant said it would have generated about $1 million in annual tax revenue.
— Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

Kia is eyeing its fourth consecutive annual US sales record after another record-breaking October. With the new 2027 EV3 arriving, Kia is “confident” the momentum will carry into Q4 and well into 2027.
Kia extends record-breaking US sales streak in October
“With six consecutive months of record-breaking sales, Kia is accelerating toward a fourth straight annual sales record,” Kia America vice president of sales Eric Watson said on Tuesday.
Kia sold 80,008 vehicles in the US last month, up 16% year over year and marking its best October sales month ever.
Kia said electrified and hybrid vehicles drove the growth, with sales up 112% and 114% YOY, both setting new sales records.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Several Kia models posted strong YOY sales growth, including the three-row electric EV9 (+111%), Telluride (+63%), EV6 (+58%), Seltos (+43%), Sorento (+31%), Carnival (+17%), K4 (+14%), and Sportage (+12%).
Regarding its fully electric vehicles. Sales of the EV9, Kia’s three-row electric SUV, are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.
Although EV6 sales rebounded slightly last month, they are still down 39% YTD, with 7,067 units sold through October.
2027 Kia EV9 (Source: Kia)
Kia’s new entry-level electric SUV, the EV3 ( check out our review ), is now in showrooms nationwide. After it went on sale in mid-August, Kia sold 1,496 EV3s in its first two months.
The 2027 EV3 is Kia’s most affordable fully electric vehicle, starting at $29,890. That’s for the base EV3 Light model, which uses a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range.
Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.
2027 Kia EV3 (Source: Kia)
Front-wheel-drive (FWD) models have a single 201-horsepower electric motor. Upgrading to all-wheel-drive (AWD) costs $3,200 and adds a rear electric motor for a combined 261 horsepower.
All variants have a native NACS port so that drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. Charging the 58.3 kWh battery from 10% to 80% takes around 29 minutes, while the larger 81.4 kWh battery takes about 31 minutes.
2027 Kia EV3 interior (Source: Kia)
Inside, all EV3 models feature Kia’s latest ccNC (connected car Navigation Cockpit) with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.
The setup provides nearly 30″ of combined digital screens, including a dual 12.3″ instrument cluster and touchscreen infotainment, plus a 5″ climate control display.
Kia describes the EV3 as an “entry-level EV SUV that offers many of the advanced amenities of the EV9,” but in a smaller, more affordable package.

Compass Pathways revealed that an FDA filing for COMP360 will be complete “in the next two weeks,” with an expected drug launch in the first half of next year. The update follows a reported regulatory submission for Usona Institute’s own psilocybin candidate for depression on Monday.
Compass Pathways expects to finalize a rolling submission for its highly anticipated psilocybin depression drug “in the next two weeks,” the company said Tuesday, possibly providing a balm for investors after its stock dipped Monday following news that Usona Institute had submitted an FDA approval application for its own psychedelic depression candidate.
Both Compass and Usona hold Commissioner’s National Priority Vouchers (CNPVs) for their candidates—Compass’ COMP360 for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and Usona’s PSIL201 for major depressive disorder (MDD)—meaning that both could be approved by the end of the year.
Psychedelics
FDA awards priority vouchers to 3 undisclosed companies for investigational psychedelics
While the FDA did not announce the recipient names of the Commissioner’s National Priority Vouchers, the agency’s descriptions of the awarded products match those in development at Compass Pathways, Transcend Therapeutics and Usona Institute.
April 24, 2026
·

·

Read more
“Confirmation that completion of [Compass’] NDA filing is expected very soon is reassuring, especially with reports that a non-profit (the Usona Institute) recently submitted NDA filing for their psilocybin MDD program,” Stifel analysts said in a note to investors Tuesday morning.
After multiple sources reported Monday that Usona had filed a new drug application for PSIL201, Compass’ shares dipped more than 35%. RBC Capital Markets suggested this might be reason to snap up Compass stock.
“With CMPS shares down today on potential increasing competitive concerns, we see a buying opportunity given we think even modest commercial success is not being priced in to shares at these levels,” the analysts wrote in a note to investors Monday afternoon. The analysts added, “Given the size of the market - we think there is room for multiple competitors.”
Compass rebounded somewhat after releasing third-quarter earnings on Tuesday but its shares are still 23% below where they started the week, sitting at $9.01 a pop as of publication.
As part of its earnings report, Compass said it was “on track” for an expected launch in the first half of 2027, subject to FDA approval. While the timing is still to be determined, the CNPV shaves review periods from 10–12 months down to 1–2 months. This “gives us more confidence approval [for COMP360] should firmly come within the 1Q27 timeframe (if not earlier) based on prior CNPV timelines,” Stifel analysts said in a Tuesday morning note.
The analysts added that the Usona filing “will be an overhang for a bit, though CMPS remains confident with NDA completion imminent.”
While both Compass and Usona’s psychedelic therapies target depression, they are for different indications, and Usona’s PSIL201 is a bit more of a mystery, according to Stifel.
“The Usona ph3 MDD data have never been disclosed, and while Compass did not comment directly on PSIL201, they did emphasize that the COMP360 data are inherently differentiated in that they come from a highly refractory TRD population,” the analysts wrote.
In a six-week, Phase 2 placebo-controlled trial of 104 adult patients with MDD, a 25-mg dose of PSIL201 met the trial’s primary endpoint by delivering “a rapid and sustained antidepressant effect . . . compared with active placebo,” according to a 2023 JAMA publication . There were no serious treatment-emergent adverse events (AE).
Meanwhile, in the Phase 3 COMP006 trial, 39% of patients with TRD who received two fixed doses of COMP360 achieved a clinically meaningful reduction in depression severity by week six, Compass reported in August. The patients who saw relief maintained a durable response through week 26. The drug’s safety profile was comparable to previous studies, with treatment-emergent AEs that were transient and typically occurred on the day of dosing, Compass said at the time.

Neurocrine Biosciences will conduct a new study for the rare disease drug Vykat to explore dosing and safety in patients with Prader-Willi syndrome who have complex health issues.
Another patient has died after taking Neurocrine Biosciences’ Prader-Willi syndrome therapy Vykat, leading to analyst inquiries during the biotech’s third-quarter earnings call on Monday afternoon.
Clinicians and patient advocates have been sounding the alarm about serious safety events that have occurred in patients who took the product, which was approved for the rare disorder in 2025 and picked up by Neurocrine in April as part of the $2.9 billion acquisition of Soleno Therapeutics .
Neurocrine this week confirmed the newly reported death and reiterated confidence in the drug’s safety profile, urging appropriate monitoring and patient selection.
“We are confident in the benefit-risk profile of Vykat XR and believe the FDA-approved label provides clear guidance on how to use the medicine safely and effectively in the indicated patient population,” a spokesperson told BioSpace in a Monday evening statement.
Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare disease that causes an insatiable desire to eat plus a slow metabolism that together can lead to significant weight gain. The condition can also cause cognitive disabilities and behavioral challenges. Before Vykat was approved, patients had few options.
Neurocrine reported third-quarter earnings on Monday, with the investor call focusing on the safety profile of Vykat. Analysts wondered about the real-world safety reports and a recent letter from a clinician warning of safety risks associated with the drug.
Rare diseases
Deaths reported after treatment with Neurocrine’s approved Prader-Willi drug
Reports of seven deaths in patients who had taken Neurocrine Biosciences’ Vykat and the official termination of Aardvark Therapeutics’ Phase 3 trial after cardiac complications marked a tough day for the Prader-Willi syndrome community.
August 12, 2026
·
3 min read

“Neurocrine remains committed to the benefits of Vykat XR in the right patients with the right monitoring, and the franchise was resilient this quarter,” William Blair said in a Tuesday morning note.
Indeed, Vykat took home $107 million for the third quarter, helping Neurocrine to reach $1.1 billion in total revenue.
To help ease concerns, Neurocrine is planning a new study in 2027 to explore dosing and safety in patients with Prader-Willi who have complex health issues.
“We clarified on the call that this was not an FDA request, despite Neurocrine’s collaboration with the agency,” William Blair said. “There is no doubt that education and data is needed to extract value from the Soleno acquisition and return Vykat XR to a true rare disease growth product, but the cards are in place now and Neurocrine is not hiding.”
Clinicians have raised concerns in the Prader-Willi community, warning about seven deaths and more than 100 serious adverse events that have occurred in patients who received Vykat. Yesterday’s report would being the number of deaths to eight.

PARIS — The French government is kicking off a new “pact” with the defense industry aimed at fostering a national ecosystem of drone makers that can quickly make new equipment tailored to its navy’s requirements.
Minister of the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin announced the initiative on Nov. 3, the first day of the Euronaval defense trade show, describing it as a novel mechanism for “converging” the needs of the armed forces.
The plan is akin to what French officials have been doing in the race to field new aerial drones, a technology that has become a fixture so central to modern combat that militaries worldwide are reorganizing to incorporate unmanned platforms.
In a statement, the French defense ministry highlighted some of the technology areas that could benefit from the new government-industry framework aimed at naval drones. For example, unmanned platforms will play a role in removing sea mines, collecting hydrographic and oceanographic data and exploring the ocean floor at great depths.
“Mastering” the seabed, as the original French wording goes, has been a fixture in the country’s naval-technology strategy for some years. The makeup of much of the seabed worldwide remains a blind spot for governments, just as critical infrastructure installed there — data cables and pipelines — has become a target for sabotage and outright warfare in the extreme underwater domain.
To that end, one agenda item announced at the trade show by French defense officials related to the naval drone framework is the purchase of a second ROV Deep Sea drone from LD Travocean, which, weighing 3,600 kilograms, can dive to 6,000 meters. The first ROV, ordered in 2024, completed qualification trials for its intended depth last week.
Related announcements include the planned acquisition of eight A18 countermine robots from Exail, a multi-sensor underwater drone for finding and characterizing sea mines before their eventual removal.
The French Navy will also buy a second unmanned combat underwater vehicle from Naval Group — this one a “bit longer” than the first test vehicle, coming in at over 10 meters in length and weighing in at more than 10,000 kilograms, a ministry spokesman told Defense News. The massive drone is meant to stay in the water for weeks at a time.
Defense officials also signed a deal with Naval Group and MBDA here to equip France’s FDI frigates with more Aster interceptor missiles. That entails retrofitting the onboard firing capability from 16 missiles to 32 on existing frigates, and ensuring new ones are built with the 32-launch-cell magazine baked in.

Redesigned in 2024 for model year 2025, the second generation of the Nissan Kicks needed two attempts to get its rear occupant crash protection right. Further changes were implemented for crossovers produced after June 2026, helping the Kicks ace the moderate overlap crash test.
Earlier 2026 models retain the previous "marginal" rating. After June 2026, the Kicks received select rear seat and seatbelt load limiter changes designed to improve rear occupant safety in this exact crash scenario. Customers who are curious when their Kicks was produced are presented with this information on the certification label, which is affixed either on the driver door or the B-pillar.
Rather than "marginal," the 2025 Nissan Kicks scored "poor" in said test. Before going any further, it's necessary for us to highlight what load limiters actually do. In the case of automotive seatbelts, these limiters are designed to control how much webbing is released under specific crash forces. They basically manage the force the seatbelt places on the occupant's chest.
The latest IIHS moderate overlap test involving the Kicks involved a 2026 model year SV with all-wheel drive, and its result carries over to the 2027 model. Up front, the dummy in the driver's seat received "good" ratings across the board, including for neck, thighs, and lower leg protection.
Photo: IIHS on YouTube Out back, the rear passenger scored "acceptable" ratings for chest protection, restraints, and kinematics. Everything else is listed as green by the nonprofit organization, and the rest of the vehicle has a fairly good report card as well. Gifted with the Top Safety Pick accolade, models produced after June 2026 are rated "good" in the other two crashworthiness tests, for headlight performance, pedestrian front crash prevention, and their seatbelt reminders.
Even the LATCH system's ease of use is listed as "G+," but alas, the IIHS could not give the Kicks the Top Safety Pick+ award due to vehicle-to-vehicle front crash prevention. "Marginal" is the overall result in this regard, with the AEB system having trouble identifying motorcycles in the 31-mph centered test.

All trims feature a 2.0-liter naturally aspirated I4 with 141 horsepower on tap, which is connected exclusively to an Xtronic continuously variable tranny. Novartis is discontinuing a neurodegeneration alliance with BioArctic in which the companies aimed to develop a drug candidate that could cross the blood-brain barrier.
Novartis is icing out BioArctic, abandoning a neurodegeneration pact that could have been worth more than $772 biobucks for the Swedish biotech.
Just last year, Novartis paid $30 million cash to join forces with BioArctic and secure a licensing option to a potential drug candidate generated from the alliance. The deal centered around the biotech’s BrainTransporter technology, which is designed to help drugs cross the blood-brain barrier. The two companies were aiming to develop a new treatment for a neurodegenerative condition combining BioArctic’s technology with a proprietary Novartis antibody.
Now, the Big Pharma has terminated the entire agreement after discontinuing the program, according to a release from BioArctic. The biotech said the decision was unrelated to its BrainTransporter technology, which uses transferrin receptors in hopes of shuttling drugs across the brain.
“This follows a recent review of our early research priorities to focus on where we can have the greatest impact and is unrelated to safety or efficacy concerns,” a Novartis spokesperson told BioSpace in an email Tuesday morning. “We remain dedicated to innovating solutions for delivering therapeutics across the blood brain barrier.”
Most recently, the pharma exercised its exclusive option to acquire global rights to Sironax’s Brain Delivery Module platform, as announced this September. Novartis first teamed up with Sironax in July 2025, when it secured the option for up to $175 million in upfront and near-term payments.

While BioArctic is losing a major partner, the biotech’s science has attracted attention beyond Novartis, drawing in partners including Eisai , Bristol Myers Squibb and, most recently, Eli Lilly . In June, the obesity-focused pharma paid $30 million upfront and is offering up to $770 million to combine the BrainTransporter tech with its own undisclosed neurodegeneration candidate.
BioArctic is the original home of Leqembi , the Eisai-Biogen amyloid antibody that secured a 2023 approval in Alzheimer’s disease. BioArctic licensed the drug to Eisai in 2007 while maintaining rights to co-commercialize the drug in the Nordic region. Eisai later partnered with Biogen to bring the drug to market.
